title: Gradient Descent
hook: Lost in fog on a hillside, you'd feel for the steepest downhill step and take it, again and again. That's how models learn.
key_points: Gradient descent minimizes a loss by repeatedly stepping in the direction that lowers it most.
The gradient points uphill, so you move the opposite way — along the negative gradient.
The learning rate sets step size: too big overshoots, too small crawls.
Stochastic gradient descent estimates the gradient from small minibatches, making it fast and scalable.
content_html: Gradient descent is the workhorse algorithm for training models. You define a loss that measures how wrong the model is, compute the gradient (the direction of steepest increase), and then nudge the parameters in the opposite direction to make the loss a little smaller. Repeat thousands of times and the model settles into good parameters.
extra_html:
How it works

At each step you calculate the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter, then subtract a small fraction of it — scaled by the learning rate — from those parameters. That fraction matters: too large and you bounce around or diverge, too small and training drags. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) speeds this up by estimating the gradient from a random minibatch rather than the whole dataset each step.

Why it matters

Nearly every neural network you've heard of was trained by some flavor of gradient descent. It's the bridge between a loss function and an actual working model, and the intuition — follow the slope downhill — explains why choices like learning rate and batch size are so consequential in practice.

related.title: How Neural Networks Learn: Backpropagation
related.hook: A neural net learns by asking, for every weight, 'how much did you contribute to my mistake?' Backprop answers all of them at once.

related.title: Learning Representations by Back-Propagating Errors
related.hook: The 1986 paper that made deep learning possible: run the error backward through the network with the chain rule, and you get every weight's gradient in one sweep.

related.title: Loss Functions
related.hook: A loss function turns 'how wrong was I?' into a single number the model chases downhill — and the loss you pick decides what it learns to care about.

related.title: Adam: The Default Optimizer
related.hook: Adam gives every parameter its own adaptive step size by tracking the gradient's recent average and spread — and it mostly just works.

prereqs.title: What Is Machine Learning?
prereqs.hook: Instead of hand-coding rules, you show a program examples and let it find the patterns — then it handles inputs it has never seen.

flashcards.prompt: Why does gradient descent step along the negative gradient?
flashcards.back_html: The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase (uphill), so to lower the loss you move the opposite way — along the negative gradient.

flashcards.prompt: What goes wrong if the learning rate is too large?

choices.text: Updates overshoot and you bounce around or diverge
Training settles too precisely into the minimum

flashcards.explanation_html: Too large a learning rate overshoots or diverges; too small and training crawls. The learning rate sets the step size.

flashcards.prompt: How does stochastic gradient descent differ from plain gradient descent?
flashcards.back_html: It estimates the gradient from a small random minibatch instead of the whole dataset each step, making it fast and scalable.
